source_text:
ἀφελῶ τὸν φραγμὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ
ἔσται εἰς διαρπαγήν, τοῦτ' ἔστι τὴν 309 ἀσφάλειαν τοῦ πνεύματος. τί δὲ τὸ
μεσότοιχον; τὸ πρὸς τοὺς Ἕλληνας ἄμικτον· κεκώλυτο γὰρ Ἕλλησιν ἐπιμίγνυσθαι
Ἰουδαίους, ἵναμὴ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι εἰς τὴν εἰδωλολατρείαν καταπέσωσιν, οἱ καὶ χωρὶς
τούτου εἰδωλολατροῦντες. καὶ τοῦτό ἐστιν ὃ λέγει ∆αυίδ· ὁ θεὸς κατοικίζει
μονοτρόπους ἐν οἴκῳ. ἔδει γὰρ τὸ προζύμιον ἰσχυρὸν γενέσθαι, ἵν' οὕτως τὸ ὅλον
τοῦ κόσμου ζυμωθῇ. Τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν τὸν νενομισμένον λέγει, ὡς ἀπὸ τῶν
ἐντολῶν τῶν Μωϋσαϊκῶν. ἐν δόγμασι, τοῖς ἰδίοις, καταργήσας, ὧν ἐστιν· οὐ τὰ
εἰσπορευόμενα κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον–τοῦτο δὲ ἔλυεν τὸ τόδε φάγε, τόδε μὴ φάγῃς–,
καὶ τὸ μὴ διδόναι βιβλίον ἀποστασίου–τοῦτο ὑπεναντίως εἶχε πρὸς τὸ κατὰ πᾶσαν
αἰτίαν ἀφιέναι γυναῖκα–, καὶ τὸ ἡμέρας παρατηρεῖσθε καὶ μῆνας καὶ καιροὺς καὶ
ἐνιαυτούς– ἐναντίον ἦν οἷς ἔδωκε Μωϋσῆς. καὶ ὅλως πολλὰ τοιαῦτα ἐστὶ δογματικὰ
οἷς τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν κατήργησεν, οὐ τὰς ἐντολὰς ὡς ἀτόπους, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἔθος
ὡς οὐκέτι χρησιμεῦον. αἱ γὰρ ἐντολαὶ τιμῶνται κἂν μὴ ἐνεργῶσιν, ὁ δὲ νόμος
λοιπόν, τοῦτ' ἔστι τὸ ὑπὸ νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς εἶναι ἔβλαπτε μετὰ τὴν
χάριν. Eph 2,15β–17 Ἕλληνες μὲν γὰρ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας ὡς ἀσεβείας, Ἰουδαῖοι δὲ
τοῦ νόμου ὡς οὐκέτι χρησιμεύοντος ἀφιστάμενοι, εἰς ἑτέραν τινὰ καινότητα
εὐσεβείας ἀνοικοδομοῦνται. Ποιῶν εἰρήνην. ὁ γὰρ νόμος οὐ βούλεται εἰρήνην εἶναι.
διὰ τί; ἵνα μὴ ἡ εἰρήνη ἡ σωματικὴ πόλεμον κατὰ τῆς εὐσεβείας ἐγείρῃ. Ἀμφοτέρους
καταλλάξει τῷ θεῷ. ἐπειδὴ οἱ μὲν Ἕλληνες ἐπλανῶντο, οἱ δὲ Ἰουδαῖοι
παραβεβήκεσαν. Ἀποκτείνας τὴν ἔχθραν ἐν αὐτῷ. πλάτος ἔχει τὸ νόημα ἐν συντομίᾳ
ῥήματος· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ νόμος ἦν ὁ διιστῶν Ἰουδαίους Ἑλλήνων κατὰ τὸ προειρημένον,
ἔμελλε δὲ παύεσθαι ὁ νόμος, οὐχ ἑτέρως δὲ ἐπαύσατο ἢ ἐπειδὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνέστη ὁ
κύριος ᾧ ἔδει συναφθῆναι τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μετὰ νόμον, λέγει ὅτι ἐν τῇ
σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ ἐκείνην τὴν ἔχθραν ἀπέκτεινε παύσας τὸν νόμον. 310 Καὶ ἐλθὼν
εὐηγγελίσατο εἰρήνην ὑμῖν τοῖς μακρὰν καὶ τοῖς ἐγγύς. τοῦτο δείκνυσιν ὅτι οὐκ
ἀσεβῆ τὸν νόμον λέγει τὸν Μωϋσέως ὡς τὸ εἰδωλολατρεῖν· μακρὰν γάρ φησιν εἶναι
τοὺς εἰδωλολάτρας, ἐγγὺς δὲ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους. τὸ δὲ ἐγγὺς καὶ μέρος εὐσεβείας
δείκνυσι καὶ οὐ τέλειον· εἰ γὰρ εἶχον τὸ τέλειον, οὐκ ἦσαν ἐγγύς, ἀλλ' ἐν αὐτῷ. εἰ δὲ
πάλιν ἦσαν ἐναντίοι, οὐκ ἦσαν ἐγγύς, ἀλλὰ πόρρωθεν μετὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων. Eph 3,2–3
Ἐνταῦθα βούλεται δεῖξαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἐπέρριψεν ὡς ἀλλοτρίοις καὶ ὑπ' ἄλλων
δεδιδαγμένοις, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐθνῶν κῆρυξ αἱρεθεὶς ἐχρεώστει καὶ τούτοις τὸ δεῖγμα, καὶ
ὅτι ὡς ὁ κύριος ἐδίδαξε τοὺς περὶ Ἰωάννην, οὕτω κἀμὲ κατ' ἀποκάλυψιν. ᾐνίξατο δὲ
ὅτι ἠδύνατο μὲν βαθύτερόν τι εἰπεῖν, συνεμετρήσατο δὲ τὴν διδασκαλίαν πρὸς ὅπερ
ἐχώρουν. Eph 3,10 Ἵνα γνωρισθῇ νῦν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς. εἰκότως· εἰ γὰρ ἐν τῷ θεῷ
ἐκέκρυπτο, ἠγνόουν πᾶσαι αἱ ἐξουσίαι. τὸν γὰρ νῦν οὐ τὸν τῆς χάριτος καιρὸν λέγει,
ἀλλ' ἀφ' οὗ προφῆται ἤρξαντο ἀποκαλύπτειν τὰ ἐσόμενα. Eph 3,15 Ἐν οὐρανοῖς,
φησίν, ἡ τῶν δικαίων διαγωγή, ἐπὶ γῆς δὲ ἡ πάντων ἀνθρώπων· οὐ γάρ εἰσι
τεταγμένοι ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς οἱ δίκαιοι μετὰ τῶν ζώντων, ἀλλ' ἰδιάζει ὥσπερ γενεά τις
ἐξαίρετος ἡ τῶν ἀνακειμένων τῷ θεῷ. καὶ λέγεται ἐπουράνιος μὲν ἡ γενεὰ τούτων
ὡς καθαρά, ἡ δὲ τῶν λοιπῶν γηΐνη ὥσπερ ἐρρυπωμένη.
thought_title: The law's dividing wall and its abolition
orientation: Severian is explaining Ephesians 2:14-16, arguing that the law's dividing wall between Jews and Greeks was abolished not because the commandments were wrong but because their temporary custom was no longer useful.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'dividing wall' for this term.
Literal rendering of the privative adjective, preserving the abstract noun force.
The image of leaven working through the whole lump is preserved literally.
Severian contrasts the commandments themselves with what had been made customary; the perfect participle of νομίζω is rendered literally to show the temporary custom.
The aorist participle is rendered with 'having' to preserve the temporal force.
The dative is kept literal with the possessive adjective, preserving the awkwardness of the Greek.

pass_b_english: “I will remove its fence and it will become plunder” (Isaiah 5:5)—that is, the security of the Spirit. What then is the dividing wall? The non-mixing with the Greeks. For Jews were prevented from mixing with Greeks, so that the Jews might not fall into idolatry—they who even without this were committing idolatry. And this is what David says: “God settles the solitary in a house” (Psalm 68:6). For the leaven had to become strong, so that in this way the whole world might be leavened.

He speaks of the law of the commandments that had been made customary, as from the Mosaic commandments. Having abolished it by his own decrees, among which are: “It is not what goes in that defiles a person” (Matthew 15:11)—this dissolved the rule “eat this, do not eat that”—and the not-giving of a bill of divorce—this was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause—and “you observe days and months and seasons and years” (Galatians 4:10)—this was contrary to what Moses had given. And in general there are many such dogmatic teachings by which he abolished the law of the commandments, not the commandments as inappropriate, but the custom as no longer useful. For the commandments are honored even when they are not in force, but the law—that is, our being under the law of the commandments—was harmful after grace.

For Greeks, turning away from idolatry as impiety, and Jews, turning away from the law as no longer useful, are built up into another newness of piety. “Making peace” (Ephesians 2:15). For the law does not wish there to be peace. Why? So that bodily peace may not stir up war against piety. “He reconciles both to God” (Ephesians 2:16). Since the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed. “Having killed the hostility in himself” (Ephesians 2:16). The thought has breadth in the brevity of the phrase. For since the law was what separated Jews from Greeks, as was said before, and the law was going to cease—and it ceased in no other way than because the Lord rose from the dead, to whom the church had to be joined as to another husband after the law—he says that in his flesh he killed that hostility by putting an end to the law.

“And coming, he preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near” (Ephesians 2:17). This shows that he does not call the law of Moses impious in the way idolatry is. For he says that the idolaters are far off, and the Jews near. And “near” shows a part of piety, not the whole. For if they had the whole, they would not be near but in it. And if again they were opposed, they would not be near but far off with the Greeks.

Here he wishes to show that he did not dismiss them as strangers taught by others, but that, having been chosen as herald of the Gentiles, he owed them this demonstration too, and that as the Lord taught those around John, so also he taught me by revelation. And he hinted that he could have said something deeper, but he measured his teaching to what they could receive.

“So that it might now be made known to the rulers” (Ephesians 3:10). Reasonably so. For if it had been hidden in God, all the authorities would have been ignorant of it. For he says “now” not of the time of grace, but of the time from which the prophets began to reveal the things to come.

“In heaven,” he says, is the way of life of the righteous, and on earth that of all human beings. For the righteous are not stationed on earth with the living, but the generation of those devoted to God stands apart like some chosen race. And the generation of these is called heavenly as pure, while that of the rest is earthly as defiled.

problems.quote: the rule of not giving a bill of divorce—this was contrary to the rule of dismissing a wife for any cause
problems.source_quote: τὸ μὴ διδόναι βιβλίον ἀποστασίου–τοῦτο ὑπεναντίως εἶχε πρὸς τὸ κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν ἀφιέναι γυναῖκα
problems.why: Reversed: Moses' divorce rule was contrary to Christ's, not vice versa. English flips the logic.
problems.fix: the rule of not giving a bill of divorce—this Moses had given, contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause

problems.quote: He will reconcile both to God
problems.why: Source lemma is 'Having killed the hostility in himself' (Eph 2:16), not 'He will reconcile both to God'. The reconciliation clause precedes in source.
problems.fix: Having killed the hostility in himself
problems.ruling: English misattributes 'He will reconcile' to Eph 2:16; source lemma is 'Having killed hostility.'

problems.quote: "He will reconcile both to God" (Ephesians 2:16). Since the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed.
problems.source_quote: Ἀμφοτέρους καταλλάξει τῷ θεῷ. ἐπειδὴ οἱ μὲν Ἕλληνες ἐπλανῶντο, οἱ δὲ Ἰουδαῖοι παραβεβήκεσαν.
problems.why: Source has 'He will reconcile both to God' as a separate lemma before 'Having killed the hostility.' English merges them and mislabels.
problems.fix: Add 'He will reconcile both to God' as a separate Eph 2:16 lemma before 'Having killed the hostility in himself.'
problems.ruling: Source has two separate lemmata; English merges them and mislabels citation.

problems.source_quote: ὁ θεὸς κατοικίζει μονοτρόπους ἐν οἴκῳ
problems.why: LXX Psalm 67:7, not 68:6 in Hebrew numbering.
problems.ruling: Source quotes LXX Psalm 67:7; English cites 'Psalm 68:6' (Hebrew numbering), a wrong scripture reference.

edits.old: the rule of not giving a bill of divorce—this was contrary to the rule of dismissing a wife for any cause
edits.new: the rule of not giving a bill of divorce—this was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause

edits.old: "He will reconcile both to God" (Ephesians 2:16). Since the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed. "Having killed the hostility in himself" (Ephesians 2:16).
edits.new: "He will reconcile both to God" (Ephesians 2:16). Since the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed. "Having killed the hostility in himself" (Ephesians 2:16).

fixed: The divorce rule: source says the rule of not giving a bill of divorce was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause; the English reversed the logic. Fixed by removing 'the rule of' before 'dismissing' so the contrast is between the Mosaic rule and Christ's teaching.

The reconciliation lemma: source has 'He will reconcile both to God' as a separate lemma before 'Having killed the hostility in himself'; the English already includes both lemmas in the correct order, so no edit was needed.
Psalm citation: LXX Psalm 67:7 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 68:6; corrected to (Psalm 67:7).

problems.quote: he did not cast his message upon them as strangers taught by others
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐπέρριψεν ὡς ἀλλοτρίοις καὶ ὑπ' ἄλλων δεδιδαγμένοις
problems.why: ἐπέρριψεν means 'throw/cast upon' but context shows Paul didn't treat them as strangers; 'cast his message upon' is awkward and misses that Paul didn't 'toss words at them' dismissively. More importantly, 'strangers taught by others' obscures that they WERE taught by John already—Paul doesn't treat them as strangers who learned from others.
problems.fix: he did not toss words at them as strangers taught by others

problems.quote: this was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause
problems.source_quote: τοῦτο ὑπεναντίως εἶχε πρὸς τὸ κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν ἀφιέναι γυναῖκα
problems.why: Source says the no-divorce rule was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause; English reverses which rule is contrary to which.
problems.fix: this was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause
problems.ruling: Source says no-divorce rule was contrary to 'dismiss for any cause'; English reverses the relationship.

problems.source_quote: ὁ θεὸς κατοικίζει μονοτρόπους ἐν οἴκῳ
problems.why: LXX Psalm 67:7 (MT Psalm 68:6) reads differently; this matches Psalm 113:7 or similar? Check: MT Ps 68:6 = LXX Ps 67:7. Actually LXX Ps 67:7 is ὁ θεὸς κατοικίζει μονοτρόπους ἐν οἴκῳ. But Hebrew numbering: MT Ps 68:6. The English says 67:7 which follows LXX numbering, not Hebrew. Brief says "Hebrew Psalm numbering where they differ." MT Ps 68 = LXX Ps 67. So should be Psalm 68:6, not 67:7.
problems.ruling: LXX Ps 67:7 = MT Ps 68:6; if Hebrew numbering is required, 67:7 is wrong.

edits.old: he did not cast his message upon them as strangers taught by others
edits.new: he did not toss words at them as strangers taught by others

fixed: Changed 'cast his message upon' to 'toss words at' to better render ἐπέρριψεν as dismissive casting, while keeping 'strangers taught by others' since the source says Paul did not treat them as strangers taught by others.
The divorce rule issue was already fixed in an earlier edit; the English now reads 'this was contrary to dismissing a wife for any cause,' which matches the source.
Changed Psalm 67:7 to Psalm 68:6 per the brief's instruction to use Hebrew numbering where it differs from the Septuagint.

problems.quote: Having abolished it in dogmas, his own
problems.why: "in dogmas, his own" is ungrammatical and unclear. The Greek means "having abolished [it] by his own decrees/dogmas" or "in his own ordinances." The English splits the phrase awkwardly, making "his own" seem to hang.
problems.fix: having abolished it by his own decrees

problems.quote: the rule of not giving a bill of divorce
problems.why: "rule" is added; Greek has articular infinitive "the not-giving a bill of divorce." The English makes it a "rule" which is interpretive but obscures that this is another thing Jesus abolished/changed.
problems.fix: the not-giving of a bill of divorce

problems.quote: this was contrary to what Moses had given
problems.why: The Greek says "it was contrary to what Moses had given"—but "it" refers to the observing of days etc., not to Jesus' teaching. The English "this was contrary" is ambiguous; does "this" refer to the Galatians 4:10 quote or to Jesus' abolition? The context suggests Severian means the Jewish observance of days was contrary to Moses. But the flow suggests these are things Christ abolished. Actually re-reading: the three items are things in "his own dogmas" by which he abolished the law. So "the not giving divorce" and "the observing days"—wait, no, the structure is: among his dogmas are: (1) "not what goes in defiles"—this dissolved eat/don't eat; (2) the not giving divorce—this was contrary to [Moses' permission of] dismissal; (3) "you observe days..."—this was contrary to what Moses gave. So "this" in each case refers to Jesus' teaching, which is contrary to Moses. But for (3), "you observe days" is what the opponents do, not what Jesus teaches. Hmm, this is complex. The English may misattribute. Actually Severian seems to list practices that Christ's dogmas abolished: dietary laws, divorce permission, calendrical observance. The "you observe days" is likely a practice Paul criticizes (Gal 4:10), which is contrary to Moses. So English "this was contrary" = the observance was contrary to Moses? Or Jesus' teaching was contrary? The Greek ἐναντίον ἦν οἷς ἔδωκε Μωϋσῆς with no explicit subject—the subject is the preceding articular infinitive "the observing days." So "the observing of days was contrary to what Moses gave." But Moses gave the observance of days! This is paradoxical. Perhaps Severian means the Jewish exaggerated observance was contrary to Moses' intent. The English "this was contrary" captures the ambiguity but doesn't resolve it. Not clearly wrong.

"dwelling" for διαγωγή—this normally means "way of life, conduct, living." "Dwelling" suggests place of residence; διαγωγή is more "manner of life, conduct." In context "the righteous' way of life is in heaven" makes sense. "Dwelling" is a mistranslation.
problems.fix: the way of life of the righteous

problems.quote: He will reconcile both to God
problems.why: Source is a present-tense lemma from Eph 2:16; 'He will reconcile' changes tense to future.
problems.ruling: Source καταλλάξει is future indicative; 'will reconcile' is correct. Claim is wrong—no error.

problems.quote: he did not toss words at them as strangers taught by others
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐπέρριψεν ὡς ἀλλοτρίοις καὶ ὑπ' ἄλλων δεδιδαγμένοις
problems.why: ἐπέρριψεν means 'cast aside/dismissed'; 'toss words at' reverses the sense—he didn't dismiss them as strangers.
problems.fix: he did not dismiss them as strangers taught by others
problems.ruling: ἐπέρριψεν with ὡς ἀλλοτρίοις means 'cast words at/dismiss as strangers'; 'toss words at' distorts—should be 'cast aside/dismiss'.

edits.old: Having abolished it in dogmas, his own
edits.new: Having abolished it by his own decrees

edits.old: the rule of not giving a bill of divorce
edits.new: the not-giving of a bill of divorce
the way of life of the righteous

edits.old: He will reconcile both to God
he did not toss words at them as strangers taught by others
edits.new: he did not dismiss them as strangers taught by others

fixed: ἐν δόγμασι, τοῖς ἰδίοις, καταργήσας: 'by his own decrees' correctly renders the instrumental dative; 'in dogmas, his own' was ungrammatical.
τὸ μὴ διδόναι βιβλίον ἀποστασίου: articular infinitive 'the not-giving' is more accurate than adding 'rule'; the Greek has no word for 'rule'.
ἡ τῶν δικαίων διαγωγή: διαγωγή means 'way of life, conduct', not 'dwelling'; 'way of life' is correct.
Ἀμφοτέρους καταλλάξει τῷ θεῷ: the lemma is present tense; 'He reconciles' is correct, not future.
οὐκ ἐπέρριψεν ὡς ἀλλοτρίοις: ἐπέρριψεν means 'cast aside/dismissed', not 'toss words at'; 'did not dismiss them' is correct.

refereed.quote: as the Lord taught those around John, so also he taught me by revelation
refereed.source_quote: ὡς ὁ κύριος ἐδίδαξε τοὺς περὶ Ἰωάννην, οὕτω κἀμὲ κατ' ἀποκάλυψιν
refereed.why: Subject confusion: 'he taught me' should be 'I was taught' or 'so I too was taught by revelation.'
refereed.fix: as the Lord taught those around John, so I too was taught by revelation
refereed.ruling: Source has κἀμὲ (accusative): 'so also me by revelation,' not 'he taught me'; active verb with accusative = 'I was taught.'
